blocks.text: A trader in Onitsha buys a carton of soap for ₦18,000 and sells it for ₦22,500. Is that a good deal? You cannot answer with the naira figure alone — you need a percentage, because percentages let you compare profits on items of completely different prices.

blocks.markdown:
A fraction, a decimal and a percentage are three ways of writing the **same** part of a whole.

- A **fraction** compares a part to a whole: $\frac{3}{4}$ means three of four equal parts.
- A **decimal** writes that part using tenths, hundredths and thousandths: $0.75$.
- A **percentage** writes it out of exactly 100: $75\%$.

Being able to move between the three quickly is one of the highest-value skills in the whole syllabus, because it appears in profit, interest, probability and statistics questions.

blocks.title: Per cent
blocks.text: "Per cent" literally means "out of a hundred". So $\%$ is just a shorthand for $\div 100$. This one fact makes every percentage conversion mechanical: to remove a per cent sign, divide by 100; to add one, multiply by 100.

blocks.caption: Conversions worth memorising — they save real time in an exam

items: Fraction to decimal: divide the numerator by the denominator.
Percentage to fraction: write it over 100 and cancel down.
Fraction to percentage: multiply the fraction by 100%.

steps.text: You can only add fractions when the denominators match. Find the LCM of 3 and 4.
Now add the numerators only. The denominator does not change.
Convert the improper fraction to a mixed number.

blocks.title: Dividing fractions
blocks.text: To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal — flip the **second** fraction only. So $\frac{3}{5} \div \frac{2}{15} = \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{15}{2} = \frac{45}{10} = \frac{9}{2}$. Flipping the wrong fraction is the single most common error on this topic.

blocks.markdown:
### Profit, loss and percentage change

Every percentage change question uses the same structure:

$$\text{percentage change} = \frac{\text{change}}{\text{original}} \times 100\%$$

The word **original** is what candidates get wrong. For profit, the original is the **cost price**, never the selling price. For a price increase, the original is the **old** price.

blocks.title: Percentage profit
blocks.prompt: A trader buys a carton of soap for ₦18,000 and sells it for ₦22,500. Find the percentage profit.

steps.text: Find the actual profit in naira.
Divide the profit by the cost price, because cost price is the original amount invested.
Multiply by 100% to express it as a percentage.

blocks.caption: Simple interest: P is the principal, R the rate per annum, T the time in years

blocks.title: Read the base of the percentage
blocks.text: When VAT and a discount appear in the same question, apply them in the order stated, each time to the amount that exists at that moment. A 15% discount followed by 7.5% VAT is $\times 0.85$ then $\times 1.075$ — not $-15\% + 7.5\%$ of the original price.

points: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three notations for the same quantity.
Per cent means "out of 100", so a percent sign is just a division by 100.
Add or subtract fractions only after making the denominators equal.
To divide by a fraction, multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction.
Percentage change is always change divided by the original value, times 100%.
For profit and loss the original value is the cost price, not the selling price.
